Papers / Visual explanation

Train a robot only in simulation, then run it in the real world.

1.7 million scripted demos in randomized simulated houses, and no real data, beat a policy trained on real robots.

Say you want a robot arm to put a banana in a black bowl, in a room it's never seen. Can a policy trained only in simulation do that with no real data at all? That's the sim-to-real problem: train in a simulator, then run on a physical robot. MolmoBot goes for zero-shot, which here means no real-world data and no fine-tuning beforehand. The authors take MolmoSpaces houses, generated by a program rather than built by hand, and add domain randomization: random lighting, textures, camera pose, friction and more, betting that variety matters more than photorealism. Scripted experts, hand-written planners that read the simulator's true object poses, record 1.7 million demonstrations for the policy to imitate. On real tabletop pick-and-place with a Franka arm, across 4 rooms and 120 trials, MolmoBot succeeds 79.2% of the time. π0.5-DROID, trained on more than 10,000 hours of real demonstrations, gets 39.2%.

MolmoBot learns by behavior cloning: it imitates the expert's actions, here with flow matching. Training minimizes L(θ)=E(o,ℓ,q,A)∼D,  τ,  ϵ[∥vθ(Aτ,τ,o,ℓ,q)−(A−ϵ)∥2],Aτ=τA+(1−τ) ϵ\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(o,\ell,q,A)\sim\mathcal{D},\;\tau,\;\epsilon}\Big[\big\|v_\theta(A^\tau, \tau, o, \ell, q) - (A - \epsilon)\big\|^2\Big], \quad A^\tau = \tau A + (1-\tau)\,\epsilonL(θ)=E(o,ℓ,q,A)∼D,τ,ϵ​[​vθ​(Aτ,τ,o,ℓ,q)−(A−ϵ)​2],Aτ=τA+(1−τ)ϵL(θ)=E(o,ℓ,q,A)∼D,  τ,  ϵ[∥vθ(Aτ,τ,o,ℓ,q)−(A−ϵ)∥2]Aτ=τA+(1−τ) ϵ\begin{aligned}\mathcal{L}(\theta) &= \mathbb{E}_{(o,\ell,q,A)\sim\mathcal{D},\;\tau,\;\epsilon}\Big[\big\|v_\theta(A^\tau, \tau, o, \ell, q) - (A - \epsilon)\big\|^2\Big]\\ A^\tau &= \tau A + (1-\tau)\,\epsilon\end{aligned}L(θ)Aτ​=E(o,ℓ,q,A)∼D,τ,ϵ​[​vθ​(Aτ,τ,o,ℓ,q)−(A−ϵ)​2]=τA+(1−τ)ϵ​ Here D\mathcal{D}D is the simulated Franka demonstrations, ooo the images from a wrist camera and one external camera, ℓ\ellℓ the instruction, for example “put the banana in the black bowl”, and qqq the joint angles. AAA is the expert's next 16 actions, each a set of joint-position targets, called an action chunk. A mixing time τ\tauτ between 0 and 1 blends it with Gaussian noise ϵ\epsilonϵ of the same shape into the noisy chunk AτA^\tauAτ. At τ=0\tau = 0τ=0 the chunk is pure noise, and at τ=1\tau = 1τ=1 it's the expert's chunk. The action head vθv_\thetavθ​, a DiT (diffusion transformer) that reads the Molmo2 vision-language model layer by layer, predicts the direction from the noise toward the clean chunk. At run time, the policy follows vθv_\thetavθ​ in small steps from pure noise to a clean chunk, runs 8 of its 16 actions, then predicts a new chunk. The action head is cheap next to the vision-language model, so the authors draw 8 values of τ\tauτ per example and train on them in parallel. Nothing in the loss mentions the real world. The policy only imitates a scripted expert in randomized simulations, so whatever works on the real robot was learned from simulated data.
